note.explanation: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. Their electron arrangements are the same, so they have almost the same chemical properties; their different masses can give them different physical properties.
examples: Hydrogen isotopes are ¹₁H, ²₁H and ³₁H. They each have one proton, but have zero, one and two neutrons respectively.
Carbon isotopes ¹²₆C, ¹³₆C and ¹⁴₆C each have six protons, but have six, seven and eight neutrons respectively.
note.checkAnswer: They have the same number of electrons, so their chemical properties are almost the same. Their different numbers of neutrons give them different masses and physical properties.
note.simple: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Same electrons means almost the same chemical behaviour; different masses can mean different physical properties.
note.checkQuestion: Why do isotopes of an element have almost the same chemical properties but different physical properties?
note.title: Isotopes and their properties
steps: Check that the atoms have the same atomic number: they are the same element.
Compare their neutron numbers: different neutron numbers mean different mass numbers.
Remember that chemical properties depend on electrons, while adding neutrons changes the atom's mass.
note.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons. Their chemical properties are almost the same because they have the same number of electrons; their physical properties can differ because their masses differ.

written.finalAnswer: Radiation from a radioactive source can collide with an atom and force an electron away if it has enough energy to remove the tightly bound electron. The atom then becomes a positively charged ion, or cation.

written.finalAnswer: Radioactivity is the process of emission of radiation by an unstable isotope. Radioactive isotopes are used for medical imaging, radiocarbon dating, and testing the strength of metals and concrete mixtures.

examTips: Short questions may ask you to define isotopes or radioactivity, identify a radioactive isotope such as tritium, or calculate neutrons using mass number minus atomic number.
For explanations, connect the same electron number to similar chemical properties and different neutron numbers to different masses and physical properties.
For a question about radioactive-isotope applications, state each use clearly and include a short detail, such as carbon-14 dating organic remains or technetium–99m imaging organs.
For ionization, show the sequence: radiation removes an electron, the atom loses negative charge, and a cation forms.

explain.title: Isotopes
explain.body: All atoms of the same element have the same atomic number, but their mass numbers can differ because their nuclei contain different numbers of neutrons. Atoms of the same element having different number of neutrons in their nuclei are called isotopes. For example, ¹²₆C, ¹³₆C and ¹⁴₆C are carbon isotopes.

explain.title: Chemical and physical properties
explain.body: The isotopes of an element have the same number of electrons, so they show almost the same chemical behaviour. Their different neutron numbers give them different masses, so their physical properties may differ.

explain.title: Radioactivity and decay
explain.body: Several isotopes have unstable nuclei and emit excess energy as radiation. This emission is called radioactivity, and an isotope that emits energy is called a radioactive isotope. When a radioactive element emits radiation and changes into another element, the process is called radioactive decay.

explain.title: Uses and ionization
explain.body: Radioactive isotopes are used in medical imaging, radiocarbon dating and other applications. Radiation with enough energy can remove an electron from an atom. The atom then becomes a positively charged ion called a cation.

mistakes: Do not say isotopes have different numbers of protons; the proton number is the same for isotopes of one element.
Do not confuse mass number with atomic number. To find neutrons, subtract atomic number from mass number.
Do not say all isotopes are radioactive; the section gives stable hydrogen isotopes as well as radioactive tritium.
When explaining ionization, include both electron loss and the resulting positive ion or cation.
For radiocarbon dating, say it is used to estimate the age of organic material; an older sample contains less carbon-14.
